extracted.intended_audience: historians of mathematics, historians of science, and mathematicians interested in the history and practice of mathematical research and publishing
extracted.subtask_description: A collection of conference talk abstracts on historical topics in mathematics (early 20th century): development of research objects, publishing practices, computational adoption, wartime mathematics, and community internationalization. The page presents historiographical analyses and case studies rather than a how-to manual.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of the mathematical advisor in publishing decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishers increasingly sought the advice of mathematicians to decide what to publish; the mathematical advisor functioned as an (often informal but influential and sometimes paid) institution in the publishing process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or organizing mathematical publishing programs, include domain experts as advisors to assess scholarly quality and potential authors. Note historical shifts (pre-WWI advisors prominent; post-WWI the advisor role changed).

rubrics_metrics.name: Transform formal knowledge into working knowledge (accessibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical books should be accessible not only to mathematicians but to a larger audience; this often requires foregoing fully formal or complete representations and instead communicating essentials so the work can serve as working knowledge for other disciplines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors/authors aiming for cross-disciplinary impact should codify and present the essentials, prioritize pedagogical clarity, and accept abridgement of formal completeness to improve usability — Courant's stance and the success of certain Springer series (e.g., Grundlehren) are cited as examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic viability and market considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Quality alone is insufficient for publication; publishers consider profitability and marketability. Decisions to publish mathematics (or to withdraw from it) are affected by sales potential and access to new markets (e.g., engineers, physicists).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess prospective audience size, possible markets outside pure mathematics, and potential sales when planning publishing programs; historical examples: Teubner's retreat from mathematics and Springer's active entry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Codification: what knowledge is needed and how to encode it
rubrics_metrics.description: A central publishing problem is determining which knowledge should be codified and in which form to make it teachable, learnable, usable, and saleable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors and authors must make explicit choices about scope, depth, level of rigor, and didactic devices to transform formal research into usable texts (textbooks, readers, manuals).

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience calibration and boundary management
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain careful awareness of the boundary between mathematics proper and its external users; choose an appropriate level (e.g., 'Lesebuch' reader vs. 'Lehrbuch' textbook) to fit the intended audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tailor exposition, examples, and formalism to the target readership; Trefftz's remark on producing a mathematical reader rather than a textbook illustrates tensions between specialist expectations and user needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify phases in research-object formation (historiographical criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: In historical analysis of mathematical development, trace phases in which mathematical entities change role: from objects under investigation, to geometrical/methodological tools prompting new questions, to being research objects themselves (e.g., Minkowski: quadratic forms → lattices → convex bodies).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analysing a research episode, look for shifts in (a) what functions as the prompting object, (b) what functions as method/tool, and (c) when a concept becomes an autonomous object of study; use these shifts to structure narrative and explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disciplinary ethos favoring conceptual methods over computation
rubrics_metrics.description: In number theory (and other 'pure' fields), there has been a prevailing ethos to develop conceptual tools and to avoid 'blind calculations'; this cultural norm affected the reception and adoption of electronic computation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When planning computational projects or advocating computing resources in such disciplines, address cultural resistance by emphasizing conceptual payoffs and integrating computation with theoretical insight (Lehmers as pioneering exceptions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Selecting computational problems as tests of new machines
rubrics_metrics.description: Classical number-theoretic computational problems were treated as suitable tests of the computing power and programming skill of early electronic machines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use well-posed, benchmark-like problems that both stress hardware/software and produce publishable, verifiable mathematical data to justify computational resources and demonstrate value to skeptical audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for mathematicians' practical wartime contributions
rubrics_metrics.description: During wartime, mathematicians were valued when they could (1) transform theoretical skills into usable computations/experiments, (2) analyze and quantify errors in approximation methods, and (3) develop improved tabular and procedural methods (e.g., GHM method in ballistics).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize pragmatism, clear error analysis, and the production of usable computational procedures or tables when engaging with applied or military bodies; demonstrate how theoretical refinements yield operational improvements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional strategies to internationalize a mathematical community
rubrics_metrics.description: To transform a national mathematical community into an international one: (a) increase visibility through international congresses (ICM), (b) found or participate in international organizations (IMU), (c) recruit leading international scholars, and (d) promote international teaching and lecture tours.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Community leaders seeking internationalization should pursue institutional hosting of international events, build and staff international bodies, make strategic hires of prominent foreign researchers, and foster cross-border collaborations and exchanges (Marshall Stone's program).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sustaining university–military/industrial collaborations post-crisis
rubrics_metrics.description: The wartime integration of university scientists into military research bodies created hybrid computing and experimental practices; these relationships became permanent postwar, reshaping institutional collaborations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or planning applied-research partnerships, recognize the long-term institutional effects of crisis-driven collaborations and design channels to maintain constructive exchanges of expertise after the immediate need has passed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pedagogical aim to broaden engagement with emerging fields
rubrics_metrics.description: To grow a research field (e.g., probability), produce accessible expositions that convince mathematicians of the field's importance; the goal is to increase the number of researchers even if the initial works do not advance physical theory directly (Borel's strategy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors and educators should prioritize convincing, accessible introductions and arguments for importance to recruit practitioners; acceptance may require lowering technical thresholds and emphasizing conceptual and application-oriented motivations.
